title: Children of the Great Depression
text:
In the early 1930s, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, began following a group of children born around 1920 and 1921 in Oakland, California. They gathered detailed records on their families, schooling, health and personalities. A few years later, the Great Depression hit, and many of the families lost much of their income.

Decades later, the sociologist Glen Elder returned to these records. He compared children whose families had suffered heavy economic losses with children from families that had come through relatively unharmed, within both the middle class and the working class.

He found that hardship had changed the children's lives, but not always for the worse. In families that lost income, children were drawn into the household economy earlier. Boys often took paid jobs, while girls took on more of the housework and care of siblings. These young people grew more responsible and more oriented toward adult roles. As adults, many of the men from deprived families were strongly committed to work and family life, and many achieved as much as their peers or more.

Elder published the findings in 1974 as Children of the Great Depression. The book helped found the life course approach, which studies how historical events shape people differently depending on their age and family when the events occur.
lesson: Shared hardship can build responsibility and strength in children when they are given real roles. Do not shield children from every family struggle; let them help.
source: Elder, G. H. (1974). Children of the Great Depression: Social Change in Life Experience. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
caveat: Elder's later comparison with a younger Berkeley cohort found that children who were very young when hardship struck fared worse, so the effect depended on age.
